title: Misnaming Memory
content_html:
Misnaming Memory

Whilst the self acknowledges the past (how I became) it seems primarily concerned with the present (how I feel now). If Memory does not belong to the self, the self belongs to memory, then this suggests that memory itself is more concerned with the present and future than being an accurate record of the past? Ultimately, calling it ‘memory’ is to misname it?

What we call memory is less an archive of the past than a real-time process of temporal inference: the brain constructs present coherence and plausible futures by reusing and revising traces of prior experience. In this sense, the self is not the owner of memory; rather, it is a momentary equilibrium within memory’s ongoing work of maintaining continuity.

The felt priority of “how I am now” reflects memory’s optimization for current stability and near-future viability. Narrative continuity (the past) is produced instrumentally to support the present—thus the self appears present-centered because it is memory’s current best model of me-in-context.

Alternatives like adaptive continuity, temporal inference, or remembrance-as-process gesture closer to the phenomenon, though none have the cultural resonance of “memory.” As with “sunrise,” the term persists even while our understanding inverts: the sun does not rise; the earth turns. Memory does not replay; it re-creates.

  1. Constructive remembering. Recollection actively reconstructs experiences by re-binding distributed cortical traces under hippocampal guidance; it is model completion, not file retrieval. [Schacter & Addis, 2007]
  2. Reconsolidation. Each act of recall renders a memory labile and subject to updating before being stored again, evidencing a present-oriented function. [Nader, Schafe, & LeDoux, 2000]
  3. Predictive use. Under the Free-Energy/Predictive Processing view, perception, memory, and imagination are degrees of the same prediction machinery operating over different horizons. [Friston, 2010; Clark, 2016]
